sections.overview: Triatoma infestans is a blood-feeding triatomine bug and an important vector of Chagas disease in South America.
sections.identification: Adults are brown-black, with pale transverse markings along the abdomen; females are about 25–30 mm long and males 21–26 mm.
sections.habitat: It is mainly domestic or peridomestic, sheltering in wall cracks, thatched roofs and animal enclosures.
sections.diet: Nymphs and adults feed on blood; after feeding, an infected bug can pass the parasite in its feces rather than through the bite itself.
sections.behavior: It hides during the day and usually comes out to feed at night.
sections.reproduction: In Argentina, the egg-to-adult cycle is reported to take about eight months to one year, depending on conditions.
sections.ecology: It acquires Trypanosoma cruzi from infected hosts and can spread it when feces contaminate a bite wound or mucous membrane.
sections.conservation: The public-health sources consulted focus on vector control and Chagas prevention, not a conservation assessment.
